paragraphs.heading: Building blocks of matter
paragraphs.text: Atoms are the fundamental building blocks of matter, and the basic particles that make up each chemical element. Each has a nucleus of protons, generally with neutrons too, surrounded by a swarm of electrons held in place by electromagnetism. The number of protons decides which element an atom is: any atom with 11 protons is sodium, and any with 29 is copper. Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are isotopes of one element.

paragraphs.heading: How small atoms are
paragraphs.text: Atoms are tiny, typically about 100 picometers across. A human hair is roughly a million carbon atoms wide. Even the shortest wavelength of visible light is bigger than an atom, so ordinary microscopes cannot show them. At this scale quantum effects take over, and classical physics cannot accurately predict how atoms behave. More than 99.94% of an atom's mass sits in its nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: Charge and ions
paragraphs.text: Protons carry a positive charge and neutrons carry none, so the nucleus is positive. Electrons are negative, and that opposite charge is what holds them to the nucleus. When an atom has as many electrons as protons, as is normal, it is neutral overall. An atom with a net charge is called an ion: extra electrons make a negative ion, or anion, and more protons than electrons make a positive ion, or cation.

paragraphs.heading: Forces in the nucleus
paragraphs.text: Inside the nucleus, the nuclear force pulls protons and neutrons toward each other. It is usually stronger than the electromagnetic push between the positively charged protons. Under certain conditions, though, that push wins. The nucleus then splits apart and leaves behind different elements, which is one form of nuclear decay.

paragraphs.heading: Bonds and change
paragraphs.text: Atoms can link to other atoms through chemical bonds, forming compounds such as molecules or crystals. Atoms joining and separating in this way lies behind most of the physical changes seen in nature. Chemistry is the science that studies those changes.

paragraphs.heading: From uncuttable to Dalton
paragraphs.text: The word atom comes from atomos, meaning uncuttable, a term used by the Greek philosophers Leucippus and Democritus in the 5th century BC. Their idea rested on philosophical reasoning, not scientific evidence, and modern atomic theory is not built on it. In the early 1800s John Dalton gathered experimental data and found a pattern now called the law of multiple proportions: when two elements form several compounds, the amount of one per measure of the other varies between them by ratios of small whole numbers. This suggested that each element combines in multiples of a basic unit of weight unique to it, and Dalton named those units atoms.

paragraphs.heading: The tin oxide clue
paragraphs.text: Tin forms two oxides. A grey powder is 88.1% tin and 11.9% oxygen, while a white powder is 78.7% tin and 21.3% oxygen. For every 100 g of tin, that works out to about 13.5 g of oxygen in the grey one and about 27 g in the white, a ratio of 1:2. Dalton read this as one oxygen atom per tin atom in the grey oxide and two per tin atom in the white: SnO and SnO₂.
